verdict.tagline: A sprawling survival sandbox where monster taming meets deep automation.
for_you_if: you enjoy combining survival crafting and automation
you want a sprawling open world to explore with creatures
you love building and managing monster bases
not_for_you_if: you expect clear combat tutorials early on
you want a fast paced progression curve without resource grinds
you need stable performance on the Steam Deck
you are sensitive to server lag during multiplayer

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Players find the mix of genres engaging despite a steep learning curve and rapid progression unlocks.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game combines monster collecting, survival crafting, automation, and RPG elements.

citations.review_text: Palworld tries to be too many things. A monster collector, a survival crafting game, an automation game, even an RPG of sorts. But it only does one of those well and it's the monster collecting. The collecting is fine and the variety of pals is basically what you'd expect if you know what pokemon is. That's the good of this game. It lacks too many QOL features for automation and crafting in my opinion. To name some, telling your pals to do specific tasks, like making transporters transport only specific items to specific chests just isn't really possible or even assigning gardeners to specific plots also doesn't exist. I've heard some of the late game crafts can take an insanely long time to craft even with pals made specifically for crafting to where you just have to find something to do in end game to wait for one item at times. I haven't experienced this personally but just what I've heard from other players. Palworld also tries to be an RPG. It has character stats but in reality only like 3 of them matter. Weight, work speed and stamina. Health does too but you can just dodge if you have half a brain and put points in stamina. Attack is a useless skill and I assume a noob trap. Palworld gives you the illusion of free will for your character. You will never be the main damage or even do significant damage, even memorable damage, it's all your pals. To make your pals stronger you have to catch unironically at least 100 of the same pal, multiply that by 5 for each party member and you have to farm 500 of the same pal to make your team stronger. That doesn't even take in account for if you want to switch a pal for a different one. That same logic goes for you base pals too that do all the automation of your base. If you want them to have better mining or handywork you have to catch an excessive amount of the same pal just to upgrade them. The way upgrading your pals and even your own gear is just such a time consuming and tedious thing that it ruins the flow of game…

[h2]Ark meets Pokémon, and it surprisingly works[/h2]

I had my doubts about [b]Palworld[/b] and held off on playing it for a long time, but after finally being convinced to try it, I have to admit: it is a genuinely good Survival RPG and a lot of fun. 

To be completely honest, if you look at it closely, there isn't really anything revolutionary or brand new here. The mechanics are things we have all seen before in other games. However, the way they blend them together is what makes it click. It truly feels like "Ark meets Pokémon," and it executes that formula surprisingly well.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]What makes it fun:[/h3]
[list]
[*] [b]The Creature Collection & Base Management loop:[/b] Catching creatures (Pals) isn't just for show. Putting them to work at your base brings in a surprising colony-sim management layer—very reminiscent of games like [i]RimWorld[/i] or [i]Frostpunk[/i]—where you actually have to monitor, feed, and manage the sanity, health, and happiness of your "workers" to keep production running smoothly.
[*] [b]Solid Survival RPG mechanics:[/b] Exploration, building, and leveling up your character keep you constantly engaged, offering a great sense of progression as you unlock better gear and technology tiers.
[*] [b]Immediate addiction:[/b] Despite its derivative nature, it hooks you right from the start. It takes known concepts and refines them into a very addictive package that turns into an absolute time sink, whether you play solo or with friends.
[/list]

[h3]Areas for improvement:[/h3]
[list]
[*] [b]Lack of real originality:[/b] As mentioned, veterans of the survival and creature-taming genres won't find many mechanics they haven't seen elsewhere. It leans heavily on familiar formulas with many highlights here and there.
[*] [b]Performance and Polish:[/b] Like many games in this genre, optimization and technical polish can be rough around the edges, occasionally reminding you of its early development roots.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Final Verdict…

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the early game as lacking a combat tutorial or clear explanations of core systems.

citations.review_text:
Playing casually this game is great. Playing on normal difficulty at this point in the game I haven't had to really think twice about having the right "team" or anything like that. The first time you find yourself on a mounted Pal is a game changing experience. There is a lot of depth and I'm excited to continue uncovering the possibilities.

My 2 complaints are (1) that I feel like there should be some semblance of a combat tutorial. I haven't died but the combat makes me feel like I'm doing something wrong and I'm not sure if I'm missing something. And (2) the level progression is arguably way too fast. Just exploring and building a base I'm levelling up and there is far too much technology for me to know what to do with. In general it feels like progression is too fast early, especially with all the possibilites the game offers you.

It's probably the clunkiest survival game I ever played. It massively overcomplicates things early on, nothing is really explained. Gameplay loop and objectives in the first 3 hours were like basic MMO objectives with no thought behind them.

I'll probably check it out again in 5 years when they fix all the issues.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe experiencing technical issues including regular stutters, crashes, and performance problems on certain hardware like the Steam Deck.

citations.review_text:
Rust meets pokemon, as we all know. If you play this with the mindset of pokemon, you won't like this game, something i realised very quickly. I play on the steamdeck and the fans get very loud so some computers will definitely struggle. The main story is very bare-bones and requires the player self-regulate how fast they go through, otherwise they will be immediately out-geared. Overall very fun even in just single-player, feeling a lot like minecraft of all things when on your own.

I wish there were more character customisation options (anthro option when) and i am not a fan of the chainmail-bikini-looking armour for the fem player models. I wish i could change how my player model looked after making the world (i may just be missing it) and all the colour customisation tools show the colours as very different in-world compared to the UI.
The progression of metals is very steep, with plasteel taking so long to make. I would love for this to be just a bit quicker due to how it is pretty early on in the game- like just mid-game is too early for so much grinding

7/10 :3

I bought Palworld back when it launched into EA, played it for a few hours and put it on the backburner as it did not click with me. As it was recently released, I thought I'd pick it up again and see what's going on, and I am enjoying my time with it immensely. It has just the right mix of exploration, base building and combat.

I am also glad to see that there is mod support via Steam Workshop and it is required for some aspects. It is not on the level of Bethesda jank, but you need mods to fix some QoL and other issues.

For example, the Mercy Ring prevents you from killing Pals when you hunt to capture them. But this does not apply to fire or poison procs. What also infuriates me is that you cannot shoot down from "high ground" as you cannot lower your weapon enough, or that you get a "mod enabled" pop-up at each game start.

The UI is functional, but not intuitive and could use some improvements. Again, not to the point that it is game-breaking, only mildly annoying.

Game performance is fine for the most part. There are regular stutters when opening chests or when flying around.

Overall, a good game, especially for the price. Can only recommend.

single_points.text: One reviewer says sphere launchers that don't lock on, clipping through the world, oversized pals that don't path find correctly, or block your view entirely, and inventory management that is downright annoying are examples of jank.

citation.review_text:
Many, Many things are overcooked and overcomplicated but it's very addictive and super fun. Customizable world settings mean you can have even more fun and ignore poorly designed mechanics like item weight.

It has a lot of Jank that is hard to ignore though. "Lock on" Sphere launchers that don't lock on. Clipping through the world, oversized pals that don't path find correctly, or block your view entirely, Pals that ignore research stations unless you babysit and carry them over to it. Inventory management and storage that is downright annoying... etc

I would classify it as Palworld .89, not 1.0 as it needs more time in the oven.

single_points.text: One reviewer says almost everything you build has to fit into a fairly small circular boundary and the Pals’ pathfinding isn’t great with floors, leading to a base where everything clips into everything else.

citation.review_text:
Great game, but the pacing and the base building wore me down. I can’t recommend it for solo play.

I put 37 hours into Palworld, and the start is excellent. Catching Pals and building your own base is a great premise, and I was hooked.

The problem is how fast everything comes at you. On default settings I was level 55 after about 30 hours, and I’d barely learned how to build properly. I was hoping for some real challenge to level up, but instead I got assembly lines and rocket launchers before I understood the basics. I know I could have turned the EXP down, but the default is what most people will play, and it felt way too fast.

That’s where the base building starts to hurt. Almost everything you build is rectangular, and you have to fit it all into a fairly small circular boundary ("All these squares make a circle"). You can work around it, but it never truly feels good. The only way to make everything fit is to build upwards, and the Pals’ pathfinding isn’t great with floors. Most of the more useful Pals are also huge, so the base ends up a mess where everything clips into everything else.

On top of that, I don’t like researching games before I play so I don’t spoil them, which meant I hadn’t planned a huge base from the start. So I felt constant pressure to expand. My options were to demolish everything and start over, or move somewhere new. That killed the peaceful feeling I had at the beginning.

My verdict: if you enjoy planning and optimizing a big base, you’ll probably have a great time. If you want a relaxed solo game, the pacing and the base limits will wear you down faster than you’d expect. I’d wait for a sale.

I returned this game during early access because it would not run on the steam deck at all.  I picked it up after the 1.0 release to try my luck again, and I am so glad I did.  This was such a fun game.  I am 125 hours in, and I can see myself putting another 75 or so into it despite 100% achievements already.  Very well made and very customizable.  Multiplayer glitches out often for us, but it is still enjoyable.
